Different, Not Less

Johann de Alwis
  • Written on 19/11/2026
  • , Last updated 13/11/2026

Cite this article as:

Johann de Alwis . Different, Not Less, Don't Forget the Bubbles, 2026. Available at: https://doi.org/10.31440/DFTB.69477

SHARE VIA:

Opens this output's Altmetric details page

“I am different, not less.”

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 3:22
Instaread

Those four words, spoken by Dr Temple Grandin—Professor, bestselling author, animal scientist, and one of the world’s most respected advocates for autism—carry enormous significance. They are simple, yet profoundly powerful. And perhaps nowhere are they more important than in Emergency Medicine.

Every day, we meet children whose brains experience the world differently. Children with autism, ADHD, Tourette syndrome, intellectual disability, sensory processing differences, and countless other neurodevelopmental profiles. They arrive in our Emergency Departments not because they are neurodivergent, but because they are unwell—just like every other child.

Yet in healthcare, it’s remarkably easy to reduce people to labels.

“The ASD in Bed 4.”…….”The ADHD kid.”…….”The non-verbal teenager.”

We rarely intend disrespect, but language shapes the way we think. That child isn’t autism.

They have favourite foods, favourite movies, and favourite people. They have a sibling who steals their Lego, a grandparent who spoils them, and a parent who knows exactly which song will calm them. They may dream of becoming a baker, spend hours drawing dragons, memorise train timetables, or know every fact about Greek mythology.

Their diagnosis is part of who they are. It is not the entirety of who they are.

A diagnosis should help us understand a child. It should never define them.

No two neurodivergent children are alike.

One may seek constant movement, while another finds movement overwhelming. One may talk endlessly about dinosaurs or galaxies. Another may communicate through gestures, pictures, or by quietly placing your hand on the object they need. Some make unwavering eye contact; others avoid it altogether. Some delight in lights and movement, while others find the fluorescent lights, alarms and bustle of an Emergency Department about as relaxing as standing beside a jet engine.

The common denominator isn’t behaviour. It’s individuality.

And perhaps that’s where Emergency Medicine has the most to learn.

As clinicians, we spend our careers recognising disease, interpreting investigations, and mastering procedures. Those skills are vital.

But perhaps one of the greatest lessons neurodivergent children can teach us is to recognise humanity before pathology.

When we pause to understand rather than simply observe, something remarkable happens.

We stop asking, “How do we get this child to fit our department?” Instead, we ask, “How can we adapt our department to fit this child?” Sometimes that means dimming the lights.

Sometimes it means allowing headphones to stay on.

Sometimes it means explaining every step before we touch a child.

Sometimes it simply means listening to the person who knows that child best—their parent or carer.

These are often small changes.

But for a family who has spent years feeling misunderstood, they can mean everything.

Because when we adapt our care to meet a child where they are, we do far more than improve their healthcare experience.

We tell that child—and their family—that they belong here.

That they are welcome here. That this hospital was built for them too. Different…..Not less.

Those words don’t ask us to lower our expectations. They ask us to raise our understanding.

To recognise that there is no single “normal” way to communicate. No single “right” way to experience the world.

No single path to feeling safe.

If we can remember that, we won’t simply become better emergency clinicians. We’ll become kinder ones.

And sometimes, kindness is the most powerful treatment we can offer.
